analysis.one_liner: Gives the USDA power to order recalls of tainted meat and poultry and fine violators.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote; it died in the House Agriculture Committee when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The USDA inspects meat and poultry plants but cannot force a company to recall contaminated product; it can only ask and negotiate. This bill would let the Agriculture Secretary order a company to stop distributing and recall adulterated meat or poultry, withdraw inspectors from repeat-violation plants (shutting down their ability to sell), and impose civil fines of up to $100,000 per violation, with each day of violation counting separately. Companies would keep a right to a quick hearing and court review.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers of meat and poultry, meaning essentially every household. Faster, mandatory recalls would keep contaminated product out of grocery stores and homes, and consumer notice would reach people who already bought tainted food.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone who eats meat or poultry

how_it_helps.text: Requires any business handling meat or poultry that suspects it is adulterated or misbranded to notify the Secretary of Agriculture immediately, so contamination surfaces sooner [S2][S3].

Lets the Secretary order a company to stop distribution and recall product when consumption poses a reasonable probability of a public health threat, if the company will not do it voluntarily [S2][S3].

Allows the Secretary to require consumer notice to people who may have bought the tainted product, and to withdraw federal inspectors from establishments with willful or repeated violations, effectively halting their operations [S3].
Authorizes civil penalties of up to $100,000 per violation, with each continuing day a separate offense, enforceable through the Attorney General [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Meat and poultry processors, slaughterhouses, distributors, and retailers, who would face mandatory recall orders, per-day fines, possible loss of federal inspection, and the costs of pulling product from the supply chain. Those costs could partly show up in food prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Meat and poultry processors and distributors

drawbacks.text: Mandatory recall and nondistribution orders take effect first and are reviewed afterward at an informal hearing within two days, so a company could be forced off the market before fully contesting the government's finding, though court review is available within 30 days [S3].

Fines can stack quickly because each day of a continuing violation is a separate offense of up to $100,000, a burden that falls hardest on smaller processors even though the Secretary must weigh business size when setting the amount [S3].

Much of the enforcement depends on the Secretary's judgment of what is 'necessary' to protect the public, so the strength of consumer protections would vary with how aggressively each administration enforces the law [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the benefit is straightforward: when bacteria-contaminated meat reaches stores, speed decides how many people get sick, and the power to force a recall and notify buyers directly shortens that window. The costs fall on the industry and can ripple into prices, and the bill does give companies a hearing and court review, but the core trade-off favors the public, since the current voluntary-recall system leaves the government asking a company to pull its own product. A fair objection is that automatic fines stacked per day could punish small plants disproportionately.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2002, sent to the House Agriculture Committee, and referred to its Livestock and Horticulture Subcommittee, and no committee or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. John Baldacci, a Democrat from Maine, introduced the bill on May 23, 2002 [S1][S3].

The House referred it to the Agriculture Committee on May 23, 2002, and on June 4 to the Subcommittee on Livestock and Horticulture; the Agriculture Committee requested an executive comment from the USDA on June 5 [S1][S5].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and expired when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Meat and poultry processors are better off, because they avoided mandatory recall orders, possible loss of inspection, and fines of up to $100,000 per violation that the bill would have imposed. Consumers remain under the weaker voluntary-recall system.

for.name: Rep. John Baldacci
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to give the Agriculture Secretary mandatory recall, inspection-withdrawal, and civil penalty authority over meat and poultry plants [S1][S3].

against.name: House Agriculture Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on May 23, 2002, referred it to the Subcommittee on Livestock and Horticulture, and never reported it out or held a vote [S1][S5].

against.name: Subcommittee on Livestock and Horticulture
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from June 4, 2002 onward without action [S5].

against.name: Meat and poultry processing industry
against.what_they_did: The bill would have imposed mandatory recalls, inspection withdrawal, and per-violation fines on the industry; no industry lobbying appears in the record, but the measure died in the committee with jurisdiction over livestock without ever coming to a vote [S3][S5].

sides.party_line_note: The record shows only a Democratic sponsor and three Democratic cosponsors; with no floor vote, there is no way to see how the parties would have split.

industries.industry: Meat and poultry processors and slaughterhouses
industries.note: The bill would have removed their control over recalls of their own product, letting the USDA order distribution stopped, withdraw inspectors from repeat violators, and fine them up to $100,000 per day of violation. Consumers would gain faster removal of contaminated food; the industry would bear the cost and the loss of discretion.

industries.industry: Meat and poultry distributors, wholesalers, and retailers
industries.note: Anyone notified of an adulterated product would be required to immediately stop distributing it, and handlers would owe notification duties. They share recall costs but also benefit from knowing sooner when a product in their supply chain is tainted.
